verdict: Caution: lend selectively to re-rollers with own working-capital discipline and water-secured supply; avoid thin-margin, single-customer units until monthly data proves otherwise.
title: Jalna Steel Re-rolling & TMT: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
Jalna is one of Maharashtra's main steel re-rolling centres, making TMT bars for houses and roads [1]. The unit buys billets or scrap, heats and rolls them into bars, and sells into construction demand. **Cash is made on the spread between input cost and bar price, not on volume alone.** Margins are thin and move with billet prices, so pricing power sits with branded players who command a premium over market rate [9]. Working capital is the real exposure: inventory plus receivables, and rating reports flag moderately high working-capital needs even where bank lines support them [11]. ## What has changed now
Water is the local story. **So when a proposal lands, check the unit's water connection and source; if it depends on tankers or shared lines, ask for the backup plan before sanctioning.** The data pack is mixed: Maharashtra GST is running 2.5 pp faster than India, a local tailwind, but electricity demand is 3.5 pp slower than India, a stress signal [D]. India-wide steel output (NIC 24) grew 2.4% YoY and 3.4% Apr-to-date [D]. ## Where the growth is
Peer results show the demand is real: Steel Exchange India clocked about Rs 340 crore revenue in Q2 FY27, up about 45% YoY [6], and Rathi Steel crossed Rs 200 crore, up over 30% YoY with volume up about 28.86% [7]. **Pursue re-rollers with branded TMT, diversified builder/dealer customers, and own billet linkage; avoid single-customer converters and units with no brand pull.** Note the peer numbers are national, not Jalna-specific; local sources say little about city-level volumes, so lean on first principles here. ## How to grow safely
Structure against the working-capital cycle, not the fixed assets. **Take monthly stock and receivable statements, quarterly GST returns, and a billet purchase-versus-sales realisation sheet every month.** Set a drawing-power cap tied to inventory and receivables, and a covenant that gearing stays below the peer benchmark of 1.80x seen at Kubair [10]. Ask for the power bill each month; a fall in units consumed is the earliest sign of a furnace idling. ## Early-warning signs
- Monthly power consumption falling while sales are reported flat (monthly) -> ask for furnace log and visit the plant. - Receivable days stretching beyond the sanctioned cycle (monthly) -> freeze further drawing power. - Billet purchase price rising faster than bar realisation (monthly) -> reprice or reduce exposure. - Water supply cut or tanker dependence emerging (quarterly) -> reassess production continuity.
watch: fall >15% with flat sales -> plant visit and stock audit
stretch beyond cycle -> freeze drawing power
input rising faster than output price -> reduce exposure
filing gap or turnover drop -> escalate to credit committee
cut or tanker shift -> reassess continuity
